title: The Calculus of Value
summary:
While the title may have raised concern for readers, my main conclusion was that the
elevated US stock market valuations at the time didn't necessarily signal the existence
of a bubble, mainly because Some investors emphasize paying a reasonable price for today's earning power and others
are willing to bet on what they see as potential growth in earning power. Some investors find another company sexy and right for the future, and others think
it's a risky high flyer.

reader_summary.headline: This is The Memo by Howard Marks, the calculus of value.
reader_summary.overview: This is The Memo by Howard Marks, the calculus of value. On July 28th, I flew to South America on a plane without Wi-Fi, leaving me without email or entertainment. What was I to do but start in on a memo?

key_points.evidence_quote: Interestingly, the things I wrote during that flight turned out to be the answers to many of the questions I received from clients after I landed.

key_points.text: So writing what follows served me well.

thesis: Howard Marks argues that investment value is derived from an asset's fundamentals, specifically its earning power, which encompasses both current income and the potential to generate future earnings. He concludes that while the theoretical right price is the discounted present value of future cash flows, real-world prices are ultimately set by the subjective opinions and attitudes of investors rather than purely mathematical processes.
